justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I assumed was a starting value near 400–403. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 403 essentially anchors to recent price momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major overnight news. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 408, reflecting a mild positive drift consistent with a typical equity or index instrument in a neutral-to-constructive macro environment. At one month, I moved to 415, incorporating a longer-run drift assumption while acknowledging that a month is long enough for fundamental repricing to begin showing up in the numbers.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, the ±18-point range around 403 reflects relatively tight short-term uncertainty, consistent with daily moves of roughly 1–2% in a moderately volatile instrument. At one week, the interval widens to roughly ±32 points, accounting for the accumulation of daily uncertainty and the possibility of a discrete macro event mid-week. At one month, the interval stretches to ±65 points, which acknowledges that over four weeks, Fed communications, earnings surprises, geopolitical developments, or shifts in risk appetite can meaningfully reprice the instrument in either direction.

Several risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, an unexpected dovish policy pivot, a strong economic data surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could drive a sharp rally beyond the upper bounds. On the downside, a credit event, a sudden spike in inflation expectations, a major earnings disappointment, or a liquidity shock could easily breach the lower bounds — particularly at the one-month horizon where tail risks have more time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that these intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions and do not fully account for jump risk or fat tails. Real-world distributions tend to have heavier tails than implied by simple volatility scaling, meaning the true probability of extreme outcomes lies somewhat above what these intervals formally suggest. Readers should treat the 90% confidence intervals as reasonable planning ranges rather than hard probabilistic guarantees.
